text: Before you fit anything clever, build the dumbest forecast that could possibly work. A baseline gives every later model a bar to clear -- if a gradient-boosted model or an ARIMA can't beat a forecast you wrote in one line of pandas, it isn't earning its complexity. This lesson builds four of them, scores them, and shows how to read the results.

Mean assumes nothing ever changes -- the average of all history, repeated. Naive says tomorrow looks like today -- the last observed value, repeated. Drift is naive plus a straight line through the first and last training points, following a steady trend. Seasonal naive says this Tuesday looks like last Tuesday, repeating the last full season.

On seven hundred thirty days of synthetic daily sales with an upward trend, a weekly pattern and a yearly wave, we hold out the last twenty-eight days as a test horizon and forecast all of it at once from training data only, splitting by time, never at random.

Scored by mean absolute error: the mean baseline scored ninety-nine point five four, naive scored seventeen point seven five, drift scored sixteen point six three, and seasonal naive scored sixteen point one three, the best of the four. The mean baseline is off by nearly a hundred units a day because sales climbed well above their historical average.

Plotting all four against the actual last twenty-eight days makes it visual: the seasonal naive line is the only one that wiggles with the weekly pattern, and it never catches the upward drift -- which is exactly the gap a real model can fill.

Pick the baseline that matches the series: trending series call for drift, strongly seasonal ones for seasonal naive. Report the best simple baseline, not the weakest -- beating the mean proves nothing. And match the horizon, since baseline errors grow as you forecast further out.

Baselines are one-liners: mean, naive, drift, and seasonal naive. Split by time and forecast the whole horizon from training data only. On our series, seasonal naive scored an MAE of sixteen point one three -- the number every later model has to beat. Next lesson: exponential smoothing and ARIMA, the classic statistical models that try.
